description: CCF shared Renovate preset: third-party dependencies only (ccf-bump owns compliance-framework ones). Normal updates run every day once a release is 7 days old (minimumReleaseAge), at most 4 new PRs per repo an hour (prHourlyLimit), with majors capped by their package rule (one per visit, about 2 open); vulnerability fixes are never held by a PR limit (vulnerabilityAlerts prConcurrentLimit and branchConcurrentLimit 0). Renovate merges at most one PR per repo per run (two with its restart), so vulnerability fixes are grouped into one PR per package manager (vulnerabilityAlerts groupName/groupSlug), and branches are rebased only on conflicts (rebaseWhen). See docs/renovate.md.

packageRules.description: Runtime changes ship in a release, so they are fix(deps): the final image stage and the Go toolchain, on top of :semanticPrefixFixDepsChoreOthers (require/dependencies).

Dockerfile base images are pinned by digest (a pinDigest PR, then digest PRs when the tag is rebuilt), so a floating tag such as nginx:stable-alpine or debian:bookworm-slim picks up upstream rebuilds with their OS and runtime CVE fixes through a PR, not silently at the next build. In the final stage these are fix(deps) (the final depType rule) and join the non-major group.

Docker updates have no release timestamp: a floating tag such as stable-alpine is no version to date, and Renovate's docker datasource gives Docker Hub tags (golang, postgres, node) none either. With internalChecksFilter strict the default minimumReleaseAgeBehaviour (timestamp-required) keeps every such update pending for good, so no docker update could ever pass minimumReleaseAge: a rebuild with CVE fixes (digest, pinDigest) or a new golang or postgres tag (minor, patch) would never get a PR, only a Dependency Dashboard line. timestamp-optional lets them through; one that has a timestamp still waits minimumReleaseAge. Majors keep timestamp-required.

Indirect Go modules (depType indirect, chore(deps) by default) are linked into the binary too, so their updates are fix(deps) and release (security fixes are fix(deps) through vulnerabilityAlerts whatever their depType).

The go.mod go directive is a minimum, which every newer Go already meets, so by default Renovate never moves it. rangeStrategy bump moves it to the latest Go (minor and patch, in the non-major group with the golang image, so the builder keeps up with the go line) and it is fix(deps): setup-go builds the releases with the go line's Go, so a bump ships its stdlib fixes. When an org module raises its go line, ccf-bump moves its consumers' go line and golang images instead (docs/ccf-bump.md#golang-builder-images).
One PR per repo for every non-major update (Go toolchain, go directive and golang image included), merged by Renovate as ccf-release-bot on its next run once the required check passes.

What the preset auto-merges (the non-major group and non-major security fixes) is labelled renovate:automerge, so renovate.yml's merge pass merges it right after the run: Renovate merges at most one PR per repo per run. Not majors or OPA, which wait for a human (docs/renovate.md#the-merge-pass).

Majors open a PR for a human, labelled needs-human (docs/attention.md), and are capped so a backlog of them can't bury a repo. Renovate compares a rule's limits with repo-wide counts: prConcurrentLimit 3 lets a major open only while the repo has fewer than 3 open non-vulnerability Renovate PRs (so at most 2 majors while the non-major group is open), and prHourlyLimit 1 only while the repo has had no Renovate PR yet this clock hour (security PRs included), so at most one major per visit, and none in a visit that opens the group. The rest wait under Rate-Limited in the Dependency Dashboard (docs/renovate.md#the-org-wide-throttle).
OPA follows the api via ccf-bump everywhere else (agent, policy and plugin repos), so Renovate leaves it alone there.
In the api, OPA gets its own PR and never auto-merges: a bump forces agent and the policies to follow. Labelled needs-human.
Internal packages, images and reusable workflows are ccf-bump's, so the two tools never fight over a version.
